chapters.title: Chapter 7: Sector Rotation and Applying Sector Analysis

lessons.title: Common Sector Analysis Mistakes: A Final Checklist

body.text: Almost every expensive mistake in sector analysis comes from one habit: applying a rule learned in one industry to a company in another. Low P/E means cheap. High debt means risky. Revenue growth means demand. Each is true somewhere and dangerous elsewhere. This final lesson collects the traps in one place so you can check yourself before you invest.

children.text: You have worked through eleven sectors and their metrics. This closing lesson turns all of it into a diagnostic. Each mistake below links back to the chapter that explains it, so treat this as both a summary and a place to return to before a decision.

body.caption: The Ten Most Expensive Sector Analysis Mistakes

cells: Comparing ratios across sectors
'This bank has 8 times leverage, that is far riskier than the cement company'
Compare within a peer group that shares a business model; deposits are a bank's raw material, not its risk
Reading P/E straight on a cyclical
'A metal stock at 5 times earnings must be cheap'
Use normalised earnings across a full cycle; low P/E usually means peak earnings
Confusing revenue growth with demand
'Revenue is up 12%, business is booming'
Split it: volume versus price in FMCG, wholesale versus retail in autos, store count versus same-store sales in retail
Ignoring operating leverage
'Sales will fall 15%, so profit falls about 15%'
High fixed costs mean profit falls far more; calculate the contribution and breakeven
Treating a tailwind as a thesis
'The rupee is at a record low, buy IT'
Currency, commodity, and policy tailwinds only matter alongside demand and valuation
Trusting the sector label
'It is classified as FMCG, so compare it with other FMCG companies'
Read segment reporting; conglomerates earn money in businesses their label does not mention
Assuming defensive means safe
'Pharma and FMCG cannot really hurt you'
Defensive describes earnings, not valuation; overpaying is a risk in every sector
Mistaking many funds for diversification
'I hold four different equity funds'
Add up sector exposure across funds, direct stocks, employer stock, and your own salary
Chasing the last cycle's winner
'This sector fund has returned 40% a year for three years'
Leadership rotates; check margins and valuations against their own history before buying strength
Believing profit without cash
'Record order book and record profit'
Check receivables, unbilled revenue, collections, and operating cash flow before you believe the profit

body.title: What Most Investors Look At vs What You Now Know to Look At

columns.label: The default view
points: Last three years of stock returns
Number of funds and stocks held

columns.label: The sector-aware view
points: The one or two KPIs that actually drive the industry
Valuation against the sector's own history, on normalised earnings where cyclical
The balance sheet measure that fits the model: capital adequacy, net debt to EBITDA, or working capital days
Where the sector sits in its cycle and what the price already assumes
Total exposure to each sector across everything you own, including your job

body.title: Quick Recall: One Correction per Sector

cards.definition: Do not use debt to equity or operating margin. Use NIM, CASA, GNPA, provision coverage, credit cost, ROA, and value on price to book or adjusted book.
Do not use P/E. New business strain depresses reported profit. Use APE, VNB margin, persistency, and price to embedded value.
Do not read rupee revenue growth as demand. Use constant currency growth, deal wins, utilisation, and attrition.
Defensive demand does not mean low risk. Track US price erosion, limited-competition launches that will fade, and plant compliance status.
Do not accept revenue growth at face value. Split volume from price, and watch grammage cuts, rural demand, and the valuation you are paying.
Monthly company sales are dispatches to dealers. Compare them with retail registrations to see real demand and dealer inventory.
Revenue growth from opening stores is not the same as existing stores improving. Use same-store sales growth and store payback.
Think in EBITDA per tonne and utilisation, value on normalised earnings and EV per tonne, and treat peak-cycle expansion announcements with caution.
Ask who sets the price. Regulated returns, administered pricing, and government intervention matter more than demand.
Reported revenue lags reality. Use pre-sales and collections for developers, ARPU and subscribers for telecom, and watch net debt in both.

body.title: Spot the Mistake
body.question: Four investors explain their reasoning. Whose logic is soundest?
options: 'This steel company trades at 4 times earnings while the Nifty trades at 22 times, so it is a bargain'
'This bank has debt of 9 times equity, which is far too risky for me'
'This FMCG stock is defensive, so at any price it is a safe place to park money'
'This cement company earns ₹1,200 EBITDA per tonne against a ten-year average of ₹900, so I will value it on the average rather than the current level'
body.explanation: The fourth investor is normalising earnings for a cyclical business instead of extrapolating a strong year, which is exactly right. The first reads a peak-earnings P/E as cheapness. The second applies a manufacturing yardstick to a bank, where deposits and borrowings are the raw material. The third confuses stable earnings with a safe valuation.

body.title: One Last Decomposition
body.prompt: A bank reports a return on equity of 16.8%. Its average total assets are ₹12,00,000 crore and its average equity is ₹1,00,000 crore. What is its return on assets? Round to two decimal places.
body.explanation: Equity multiplier = ₹12,00,000 crore ÷ ₹1,00,000 crore = 12 times. ROA = 16.8% ÷ 12 = 1.40%. Always look at both numbers together: a 16.8% ROE built on 1.4% ROA and 12 times leverage is a healthy bank, while the same ROE built on 0.8% ROA and 21 times leverage would be a far more fragile one.

body.title: The Portfolio Review
body.scenario: A friend asks you to review his ₹15,00,000 equity portfolio. He holds: a Nifty 50 index fund, a large cap fund, a banking sectoral fund bought after three strong years, shares in the private bank where he works plus employee stock options, a steel company bought at a P/E of 5 at the top of the commodity cycle, and an IT sectoral fund bought when the rupee hit a record low. He says he is well diversified because he holds six different investments across four sectors, and he is worried only because 'the market looks expensive'.
body.prompt: Which mistakes from this course does his portfolio contain, and what would you suggest?
body.modelAnswer: At least five. First, hidden sector concentration: the index fund, large cap fund, banking fund, employer shares, and stock options all load onto financial services, and his salary depends on the same sector, so a banking downturn would hit his portfolio and income together. Second, chasing the last winner: the banking fund was bought after three strong years. Third, the cyclical P/E trap: a steel company bought at 5 times peak earnings is priced on a margin that may not repeat. Fourth, treating a tailwind as a thesis: buying IT purely because the rupee was weak ignores demand, valuation, wage costs, and hedging. Fifth, mistaking the number of holdings for diversification. Suggestions: add up his true exposure per sector, as a percentage of the total, before anything else; reduce the overlap, starting with the position where concentration and job risk compound, which is the banking sectoral fund; plan a gradual, tax-aware reduction of employer stock after any lock-in; recalculate the steel holding on normalised earnings and decide whether he would buy it today at that price; and deliberately add sectors his portfolio lacks, such as healthcare or consumption, rather than adding another fund that owns what he already has. His worry about the market being expensive is far less important than the concentration he has not noticed.

body.text: The most dangerous sentence in sector investing is 'I understand this industry because I work in it'. Familiarity with a business is useful for judging its operations and worthless for judging its valuation, and it usually comes bundled with the salary, bonus, and employer stock that already tie you to that sector.

body.title: Fill in the Blank
body.textWithBlank: Before comparing any two companies on a ratio, first confirm that they share the same ___ model, since the same number can mean opposite things in different industries.
body.explanation: This single check prevents most sector analysis errors, from judging banks on debt to equity to judging cyclicals on reported P/E.

body.title: The Master Checklist: Run This Before Any Sector Decision
steps: Name the business model precisely, then pick peers that share it, using classification links and segment reporting
Identify the one or two KPIs that actually drive this industry, and find them in the latest investor presentation
Decide whether the business is cyclical or defensive, and where in its cycle it sits right now
Check margins against their own ten-year range before believing any earnings number
Use the valuation metric that fits the model, on normalised earnings for cyclicals, not the reported P/E on a screener
Check the balance sheet measure that fits: capital adequacy for lenders, net debt to EBITDA for capital-heavy businesses, working capital days for project businesses
Verify that profit is turning into cash: collections, receivables, and operating cash flow
Add up your total exposure to this sector across funds, stocks, employer stock, and your own income
Write down what would prove you wrong, and the price or condition at which you would exit
Diarise a review for after the next results season, so the decision gets revisited on a schedule, not on a headline

body.text: You do not need to master all eleven sectors. Most successful investors deeply understand two or three and hold the rest through diversified funds. The value of this course is knowing which questions each sector demands, so you can tell when a stock is outside your circle and treat it accordingly.

points: Nearly every sector analysis mistake comes from applying one industry's rule to another industry's company
Low P/E on a cyclical usually signals peak earnings; normalise before concluding anything about value
Revenue growth is not demand growth until you split it: volume versus price, wholesale versus retail, new stores versus same stores, pre-sales versus reported revenue
Defensive describes the stability of earnings, never the safety of the price you pay
Sector labels hide conglomerates and mixed business models; segment reporting is the corrective
Holding many funds is not diversification; add up exposure across funds, stocks, employer stock, and your salary
Profit without cash conversion is a claim, not a result
Match the metric to the model, the valuation to the cycle, and the position size to your total exposure

body.text: This lesson summarises educational frameworks, not investment advice. All examples and figures are illustrative and hypothetical. Sector characteristics, regulations, and market structures change over time; verify current data before making any investment decision, and consider consulting a SEBI registered investment adviser for personal advice.
